schools.summary: Gill supposes a deliberate pause: Elihu waited for Job’s reply, and resumes because matters remain for him to take up, though Job had said nothing to answer.
Ellicott notes Elihu hardly keeps his professed calm, accusing Job at once; the great parade of wisdom, and Job’s own like sentiment at ch. 12:11, hint the debate is not an actual conversation.
Clarke maps the speech: exhortation to the bystanders (vv.1-4), the charge of accusing God (vv.5-12), God’s power and judgments (vv.13-30), how men should address God (vv.31-37).
Henry watches Elihu the orator court his hearers’ good-will, calling them wise, appealing to their judgment and taking them into partnership, before arraigning Job’s passionate words.

Keil and Delitzsch reason by elimination that the wise addressed are neither Job and the three nor all comers, but the circle of spectators round the disputants; Elihu takes up the word afresh since Job is silent.
Gill rules out the three friends (with whom Elihu was displeased) and irony, taking the wise men for bystanders known to be of real understanding.
Wesley glosses ‘ear’ as the mind to which things are conveyed — the summons to hear a summons to weigh.
Henry marks the courtesy: Elihu allows his hearers the name of wise even while differing (1 Cor. 10:15); peevish disputants think all fools who differ from them.
Gill reads the trying ear wholly of discernment — not the sound of words but their sense, whether sound doctrine or unsound; the hearing ear is God’s gift.

Clarke rejects Calmet’s inward-judgment-only reading, hearing the Eastern delight in euphony: Elihu labours for harmonious versification as for pious sense, like the Hebrew, Arabic, and Persian poets.
Henry makes it a rule of fair dealing: the speaker must stand the test of the intelligent, and we must let our own words be proved as we prove what we hear.

debates.question: Does ‘the ear trieth words’ mean only the testing of truth, or also the ear for the music of speech?

sides.position: the trying of sense and doctrine, a mind that will not swallow whatever it is told
also the connoisseur’s ear for euphony — Elihu labours for harmonious versification

schools.summary: Gill reads ‘choose judgment’ as taking the just side of the question, with the present controversy with Job in view.
Clarke turns it against the vices of debate: not the applause of men nor victory but correct views and the finding out of what is good.
Henry hears Elihu refuse to be sole dictator: lay aside animosity and prejudice, fix right principles, compare notes — we discern right best when we help one another search it out.

Clarke and Wesley defend Job: he called himself righteous only against the friends’ charges, not as free from sin, and meant not that God is unjust but that God dealt mysteriously and withheld a fair hearing (ch. 27:2).
Gill distinguishes the senses — Job righteous evangelically and upright, but not in himself or sinless — yet allows he thought himself too righteous to be so afflicted, as Elihu took him.
Henry records the recital as a real accusation: Job insisted on his innocence and charged God with injustice, and ought to be checked for it.
Ellicott anchors the quotation in ch. 13:18 and ch. 27:2.

debates.question: Does Elihu report Job’s words fairly, or overstate them into a charge against God?

sides.position: he flattens a sufferer’s protest — Job meant righteous only against the friends, and did not charge God with injustice
it is a real accusation Job ought to be checked for — he charged God with taking away his judgment
Job did think himself too righteous to be so afflicted, as Elihu understood him

themes: God hath taken away my judgment

schools.summary: Ellicott reads ‘wound’ literally as the arrow that struck him (ch. 16:13; 17:1), ‘without transgression’ on Job’s part, preferring the AV over ‘I am accounted a liar’; Keil and Delitzsch head the strophe with the axiom that wrong is inconceivable on God’s part.

Clarke reads a pathetic truth — Job struck without cause, as God testified (ch. 1:1; 2:3) — and lingers on ‘my arrow,’ a man of calamities without transgression; Wesley: should I falsely accuse myself of crimes deserving such judgments?
Gill supplies the answered question — should I lie against my right? No — noting Broughton’s non-interrogative reading.

debates.question: Is the first line a proud refusal or a complaint of being counted a liar?

sides.position: ‘Should I lie against my right?’ — a refusal to make a false confession (AV)
‘notwithstanding my right, I am accounted a liar’ — a darker complaint

themes: should I lie against my right

schools.summary: Clarke unfolds the camel-metaphor — a great turbid draught before the desert journey — and marks the charge a repetition of Eliphaz (ch. 15:16); Wesley reads ‘like water’ as greedily, scorn poured out against friends and in some sort against God.
Ellicott shows the same reproach was aimed at Job by Zophar (ch. 11:3) and Eliphaz (ch. 15:16) — recycled, not fresh.
Gill hears the marvel at a man once esteemed wise and good behaving so.
Henry offers three readings of drinking scorn — pouring it out, drinking in others’ scorn, or drawing scorn on himself — and prays not to be left to reproach the foolish (Ps. 39:8).

themes: a charge borrowed from the friends

schools.summary: Clarke softens the charge — Job did not consort with the profligate, but his reasoning makes a track toward their creed (cf. v.9); Wesley: I dare not call him wicked, yet in this matter he speaks like one of them.
Henry: not that Job associated with the ungodly, but in opinion he favoured and strengthened their hands; to say one has cleansed his hands in vain gratifies God’s enemies (Ps. 73:13).
Ellicott notes Eliphaz had brought the same charge (ch. 15:4; 22:15) — Elihu treads a worn path.
Gill names the company as the worst of men who make sinning their trade.

Ellicott gathers the passages behind the inference (ch. 9:22; 10:15) and turns the tables: Eliphaz virtually said the same, calling it indifferent to God whether man is righteous (ch. 22:3), which saps all morality.
Gill: not Job’s words expressly but consequentially, an inference from what he said.
Wesley: not in express terms but by consequence, because Job said the good are no less, sometimes more, miserable than the wicked.
Henry grants delight in God is true religion and pleasant, but its advantage is here wrongly denied (Mal. 3:14); Job’s ill-expressed word at ch. 9:22 gave the occasion.

themes: the danger of a hasty word

schools.summary: Henry sets the axiom both ways: God wrongs none (he can no more sin than die or lie) and ministers justice to all; he punishes only where he finds sin, never in undue proportion; being Shaddai he cannot be tempted with evil (James 1:13).

Ellicott marks the broader ground: Elihu appeals to an audience, not the friends, and rests not on the problems of God’s government but the impossibility of his acting unjustly (Gen. 18:25); God, put in charge by none, has no private interest against his creatures (John 10:12).
Clarke reads the word-order as exclamation: wickedness, far be that from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.
Gill notes the address to men of understanding, of ‘heart,’ and the aim to refute Job’s sense.

themes: the Judge of all the earth

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the connection: the axiom the friends defend, true but misapplied, is here repeated with emphatic ‘yea verily’; the verb is God’s doing evil, and the proof begins at v.13.

Henry gives the rule of distributive justice — every man according to his work, well to the righteous and woe to the wicked — meeting the delay of recompense with a day coming, ‘with interest for the delay.’
Gill takes it (with Ben Gersom) as the reward of a man’s work rendered back, whether wicked or good.
Clarke: God ever will do justice; the righteous never forsaken, the wicked not ultimately prospered.

themes: the work of a man rendered

schools.summary: Gill hears the truth affirmed most strongly, and draws the versions’ ‘will not condemn’ — God will not condemn the righteous; his afflicting is that they be not condemned with the world, no condemnation to them in Christ.
Henry weighs the warmth — asserted with assurance (‘yea surely’) and with abhorrence of the contrary; God will neither wrong any nor deny any right, the heavens shall declare his righteousness.
Wesley marks where the emphasis bites: ‘will not pervert judgment, as Job hath affirmed’ — the denial answers Job’s charge.
Gill: God is no deputy or sub-governor but sole Governor by right of creation, held from himself; with no superior to please or fear, the Judge of all the earth will do right.
Wesley: the sole Creator and Lord must have all perfections, including perfect justice; Clarke: the government of the world itself displays God’s care, justice, and mercy.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the verb as enjoining a charge (against Ewald and Hahn); Ellicott gives both senses — ‘set the world upon him’ (entrusted, none over him) or ‘who but he made it?’ — either way his interest cannot collide with his creatures’.
Henry makes it a ground of submission: the government is his, his power original, and there is no higher power to appeal to.

debates.question: How should ‘who hath disposed the whole world’ be rendered?

sides.position: ‘who entrusted the world to him?’ — implying none is over him
‘who but he made the whole world?’ — so that his interest in it is supreme

themes: who gave him charge over the earth
no superior to please or fear

schools.summary: Gill reads ‘set his heart’ of hostile intent (Jarchi, to destroy): if God dealt by strict justice none could stand, and that all have not perished proves how far he is from injustice.
Clarke reads it of love: on whomsoever God sets his heart, though the body turn to dust, the soul God gathers to himself — a promise, not a threat.

Ellicott calls the clause ambiguous — ‘set his heart upon himself’ (his own interest), or upon man to injure, in which case he injures his own; the writer knew Gen. 3:19, and Elihu speaks with entire self-confidence.
Henry keeps the reading of irresistible power: God able to crush any easily, yet forbearing, which must be ascribed to the perfection of his nature.

debates.question: What does ‘if he set his heart upon man’ mean?

sides.position: a hostile purpose to destroy — none could stand under strict justice
God’s saving love, gathering the soul to himself
God’s regard to himself / his own interest in his own creatures

themes: if he set his heart upon man

schools.summary: Gill dwells on ‘together’ — not one by one but all at once, as the flood swept the ungodly; if God take out the spirit, all flesh dies immediately.

Henry draws both sides: God can bring us to dust merely by withdrawing his sustaining providence (the air-pump), and may do so without wrong, recalling a being we hold as tenants at will and have forfeited.
Wesley reads the design of this verse and the last as one — to declare God’s absolute and uncontrollable sovereignty over all men.

themes: the humbling floor of the argument

schools.summary: Gill guards Job’s intelligence — the ‘if’ takes his understanding for granted — and notes the Jewish reading of an imperative verb, ‘understand thou now, hear this.’
Henry sets the two heads of all that follows: God is not to be quarrelled with, and God is to be acknowledged and submitted to in all he does.
Keil and Delitzsch read the call to attention as framing the coming challenge — whether one who hated right could govern, and whether Job dare condemn the All-just.

themes: if thou hast understanding, hear this
the two heads of the plea

schools.summary: Clarke: preposterous that he who lives by no rule should impose rules — God, fountain of justice, binds man by law; Wesley makes it Abraham’s and Paul’s argument (Gen. 18:25; Rom. 3:5), that the fountain of justice cannot be unjust.

Ellicott states the argument’s strength — the ultimate ruler must be fit to rule, therefore just — and mends ‘most just’ to ‘just and mighty’; Keil and Delitzsch frame the interrogative and its grammar.
Gill: one who hates right is unfit to rule, the absurdity to which Job is reduced; notes Broughton’s ‘foe to judgment’ and the sense of the verb ‘to bind’ (as binding a wound).
Henry: the Lord so loves right that even upright Job might be said to hate it by comparison — shall we prescribe to him or condemn one righteous in all his ways?

debates.question: Does the second clause turn on ruling or on binding/obligation?

sides.position: ‘shall he that hateth right govern?’ — the rule of the world proves the ruler just
‘shall he who hateth judgment lie under obligation / bind?’

themes: shall he that hateth right govern
the rule of the world proves justice
the argument of Abraham and Paul

schools.summary: Clarke guards the office over the man — even a bad ruler’s office is sacred, and to rail at the man would destroy authority; Wesley: though a king be wicked, subjects may not call him so.
Gill: not fit to call even a bad king wicked, save by prophets sent of God and with decency; ‘Belial’ means lawless or unprofitable, which a king (God’s minister for good) is not.
Ellicott names the a fortiori form — if not a king, how much less the King of kings — with a strong but natural ellipse in the Hebrew.
Henry: more absurd to arraign God than to affront majesty; we presume a sentence right unless the contrary be evident (Nathan reproved David by a parable).

debates.question: How far may even a wicked ruler be reproved?

sides.position: a bad king may be reproved, but by the right person (a prophet) and with decency
the office is so sacred that subjects dare not call even a wicked king wicked

themes: say not to a king, thou art wicked
less to greater, the King of kings

schools.summary: Gregory the Great turns the verse to the searching of hearts: God judges by desert, requiring more where he gave more (Luke 12:48), and reads prince/tyrant as every proud person and the poor as the humble whom God will vindicate.
Henry presses the comfort to Job: rich and poor are level before God, and Job now poor has as much favour as when rich, for all are the work of his hands, made poor or rich by the same providence.
Gill: God is no respecter of persons, not of kings and princes, who do not escape his wrath when they sin.
Clarke: if improper to speak against a king, how much more against God, who regards rich and poor alike as his creatures.

outliers.note: Reads the social terms allegorically — prince/tyrant as every proud man, the poor as the humble — making the verse a warning that God knows not the proud who oppress the lowly.

themes: accepteth not the persons of princes
rich and poor level before God
all the work of his hands

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the impartial hour — rich and poor die together, death neither hastened nor delayed — hears the midnight of Exod. 12:29, and prefers habitual presents to futures.
Henry meditates on God’s almighty ease: the mightiest taken from his throne in a moment, without warning, at the careless midnight (as Egypt’s firstborn), ‘without hand’ by secret judgment.
Gill spreads the leveling — kings and peasants alike struck dead without notice; the Targum refers the midnight shaking to Sodom.
Clarke reads it of Eastern tyrants who seldom die naturally, cut off suddenly at midnight by the oppressed or the angel of death.
Gill unfolds the omniscience — every man, every step, inward and outward, the thoughts and affections of the soul, good or bad, all open before God.
Henry makes it warning and discipline: the subtle cannot escape God’s eye, so when judgments puzzle us we should ascribe them to a secret cause known to him; all our goings are recorded for judgment.
Ellicott sets the attribute in the argument: God is not only just and mighty but all-wise, and therefore cannot err.
Wesley: God destroys neither prince nor people unjustly nor of mere pleasure, but for sins he sees exactly, though they use every art to hide them.

themes: his eyes are upon the ways of man
the hinge of power and justice

schools.summary: Gill: no darkness of any kind, nor any darkness in God, can hide the workers of iniquity — not even the grave, whence they shall be raised for judgment.
Clarke gives an eschatological turn: no darkness in this life, no shadow of death in the other — no annihilation in which to take refuge.
Ellicott hears the verse answering Job’s own words at ch. 24:13 (the murderer who loves darkness); Keil and Delitzsch note God makes short work without investigation, conduct at once manifest to him.
Henry draws the terror: sinners would hide as Adam among the trees, or in the grave, rather than face the judgment-seat, and would call to rocks and mountains — all in vain.

outliers.note: Reads ‘shadow of death’ of the next world, denying the wicked even the refuge of annihilation — no oblivion in the grave and no escape in death.

themes: the eye that needs no inquiry
the folly of hiding from God

schools.summary: Ellicott lays both readings side by side — ‘not so much that he should enter into judgment with God’ (AV, probably right), or ‘he needs not consider a man twice,’ God being infallible and needing no second trial.
Gill unfolds the moderation — God lays not more than right in duty, punishment, or chastisement, always less than desert — or joins the clause to God’s not appointing man a set time for judgment.
Clarke: God tries no cause twice, his sentence without appeal; man’s time of judgment is not in his own hand but with God, who will judge for the oppressed.
Henry turns it on Job: God exacts not more than iniquities deserve; no man can bring an action against him, so Job was well-advised to let fall his complaint.

debates.question: What does ‘he will not lay upon man more than right’ mean?

sides.position: God never punishes beyond desert — no cause to enter judgment with him
God, being infallible, needs no second trial and appoints no time for man to go before him

themes: none may enter judgment with God

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render ‘without investigation’ (not innumerabiles), their conduct at once manifest; Ellicott reads ‘in an unsearchable manner,’ as the ‘without hand’ of v.20 — without human means.
Gill catalogues the mighty God breaks like potters’ vessels and gives both renderings — ‘without number’ (numberless instances) or ‘without search’ (God needs no judicial inquiry).
Henry: not one but hosts of the mighty overpowered, for no combined power stands against Omnipotence; yet destroying tyranny God sets better rulers in their stead, not anarchy.
Clarke: God depresses the proud and raises the humble, so neither strength nor number gives security.

debates.question: Does the phrase mean ‘without number’ or ‘without search / unsearchable manner’?

sides.position: ‘without number’ — God breaks countless mighty men (AV)
‘without investigation / by no human means’ — as ‘without hand’ in v.20

themes: he sets others in their stead

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read God’s seeing through their works as ground of the nocturnal overthrow, striking them in the very stead of evil-doers; Ellicott notes we expect ‘because’ not ‘therefore’ — the writer reasons from God’s just acts to his knowledge.
Gill: God weighs and makes their works known — to the guilty (Cain, Pharaoh), to others by judgment (the flood, Sodom), and to all at the last day.
Clarke fixes on the sudden night-stroke: in a single night the plenitude of power is annihilated, as with Belshazzar and Babylon.
Henry weaves it into God’s dealing with tyrants — space to repent, or overthrow in the night (Belshazzar) — and the vanity of flying from a justice that knows every design.
Gill lays the weight on ‘as wicked men’ — God strikes only for wickedness (Eden, the flood, Sodom, Pharaoh), so is not chargeable with unrighteousness; notes Sephorno’s ‘instead of wicked men.’

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch prefer ‘in the place/stead of wicked men,’ God striking them publicly so none can doubt who or why; Keil dwells on the resounding blow struck on men of unimpeachable honour.
Henry gathers the purpose of publicity: humbling judgments struck in terror, an alarm in open sight that others may see and fear.
Clarke keeps the plainer sense but notes the openness — the mighty suddenly destroyed in the sight of the people.

debates.question: Does ‘he striketh them as wicked men’ mean in the character of, or in the place/stead of, wicked men?

sides.position: in the character of wicked men — marking the just ground of the stroke
in the place/stead of wicked men — marking its public, exemplary manner

themes: he striketh them as wicked men
in the open sight of others

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the clause shows Elihu, like the friends, believed in the direct execution of God’s judgments — not clear of their scheme; Keil and Delitzsch set it as the ground of the falling away, leading to the cry of the poor.
Henry anatomizes the sin: rebels who turned back, cast off God’s fear, and would not consider his ways — inconsideration the root of impiety, and it is because they will not, not cannot.
Gill reads the turning back as apostasy (Cain’s line, Ham’s), a turning from the law of God, or from the light and law of nature (LXX).
Clarke: corrupt, tyrannical rulers who departed from God in heart, conduct, and government, and would not understand his ways.

outliers.note: Hears the verse expose Elihu’s own theology — that he too, like the friends, held to the direct, visible execution of God’s judgments, the scheme the book questions.

schools.summary: Clarke draws the terror — nothing so dreadful in heaven’s court as the prayers and tears of the poor (the tale of the laird ‘prayed dead’); Wesley: their case is bad who have the poor’s tears against them, drawing down vengeance.
Henry: the tyrants who will not pray for themselves make the poor cry, and that cry against them draws down vengeance (Exod. 22:23), and none can say it is more than right.
Gill: through oppression the poor are made to cry, and their cries and tears enter the ears of the Lord of hosts.

themes: the cry that stops finds the throne

schools.summary: Clarke calls it beautiful and true and turns it to liberty of conscience — who may forbid another’s worship? — God defending the weak and destroying those who fill up their iniquity; Wesley: God works mercy or justice as irresistibly on a nation as on one man.
Henry: the world’s frowns cannot trouble those God quiets (Phil. 4:7), nor its smiles quiet those he troubles; if he hide his face, none can behold him or relieve without him (2 Kings 6:27).
Gill: peace external and inward is God’s, undisturbed when he gives it; notes the versions’ ‘who shall condemn?’ for ‘who shall make trouble?’
Ellicott fixes the wording — literally ‘who can condemn?’ — and reads ‘against a man alike,’ God judging nations and individuals all one.

debates.question: Does the clause read ‘who can make trouble?’ or ‘who can condemn?’

sides.position: ‘who can make trouble?’ — none can disturb the peace God gives (AV)
‘who can condemn?’ — the reading of the Targum and versions

themes: the sovereignty over peace and trouble

schools.summary: Gill reads the hypocrite as a political one — feigning care for the people, then a tyrant once enthroned — whom God will not suffer to ascend or to continue.
Ellicott turns it to the provocation of God, whether by an ungodly man reigning or by the snares of a whole corrupt nation, e.g. Sodom.
Wesley reads ‘reign not’ as not continuing the tyranny, God freeing the ensnared people; Clarke connects the Vulgate’s ‘causes a wicked man to reign because of the people’s sins.’
Gregory reads Elihu himself as the haughty man, whose coming show of humility (‘if I have sinned, teach thou me’) is the hypocrite’s cloak, a fishing for approval.
Henry expounds the providence: God provides the hypocrite reign not, or not long, guarding a people whose liberties are wheedled from them by tyrants who cloak ambition in religion.

debates.question: Who is the ‘hypocrite’ whose reign God prevents?

sides.position: a political hypocrite or tyrant God will not let stand over the nations
the provocation of an ungodly ruler or a whole corrupt people
Elihu himself, whose show of humility is the hypocrite’s cloak

outliers.note: Turns the verse’s light upon the speaker, reading Elihu as the haughty man whose feigned humility in the next verses is a fishing for approval, not true self-doubt.

schools.summary: Henry draws the pastoral method: reproof turned to instruction (Prov. 6:23), recommended not imposed; unlike the friends, Elihu asks Job only to own he spoke unadvisedly — to accept the rod as medicinal and resolve against sin.
Gill: meet to be said by any afflicted person under God’s chastising hand, and particularly by Job.
Clarke sums it: humble thyself and say, I have suffered, I will not offend.
Keil and Delitzsch render the clause otherwise — ‘I have been proud, I will not do evil’ — owning the pride rather than the chastisement borne.

debates.question: Does the penitent say ‘I have borne chastisement’ or ‘I have been proud’?

sides.position: ‘I have borne chastisement’ — owning the punishment justly borne (AV)
‘I have been proud, I will not do evil’ — owning the pride that brought it

themes: accept the rod, offend no more

schools.summary: Gill opens the words two ways — of God’s unsearchable dealings (‘teach me more of thy ways’) or of secret sins (‘point them out that I may confess them’).
Henry expounds it as the good man’s desire to know the worst of himself, praying God to discover unseen abominations and awaken the conscience, especially under affliction.
Clarke and Wesley keep the sense of secret sins: what I do not know, teach thou me; manifest the sins I cannot discover.

themes: that which I see not, teach thou me

schools.summary: Ellicott presses the logic: should God recompense according to thy mind? then why not mine, or anyone’s — and then he is no longer supreme; the verse is obscure from its abruptness.
Henry reasons with Job’s uneasiness: absurd and vain to expect all according to our mind, for God is Creator and will take his own way — thy wisdom is to be easy and at a point.
Gill offers the alternatives — the government of the world, or chastisement: should a man be consulted whether or how he is to be corrected?
Wesley: does God need thy advice how to govern and reward? Clarke owns the original obscure and gives Mr. Good’s paraphrase, pressing Job to choose submission or persistence and speak.

themes: should it be according to thy mind
God’s government not bent to man’s will

schools.summary: Ellicott alters the mood — ‘men of understanding will say to me / agree with me’ — a claim that the wise already side with him, not a request for judgment; Keil and Delitzsch carry the self-assurance into the coming verdict on Job.
Gill takes it as a simple submission of his case, right or wrong, to men of judgment.
Clarke and Wesley read it as a wish that the wise judge his words — ‘I am content that any wise man should judge of my words.’
Henry: let men of understanding say whether a more favourable construction can be put on Job’s words than his own, and whether Job ought not to cry, I have done wrong.

debates.question: Is the appeal a humble submission or a confident presumption of the wise men’s assent?

sides.position: ‘let men of understanding tell me’ — submitting his case to their verdict
‘men of understanding will agree with me’ — presuming their assent in advance

themes: let men of understanding tell me

schools.summary: Gill bounds the charge — not that Job was ignorant in natural or divine things, but that on this one point, the chastening hand of God, he spoke amiss.
Henry finds the censure just in this matter but softens it, retorting Job’s own rebuke of his wife (ch. 2:10) upon him — he now speaks as one of the foolish men speak.
Keil and Delitzsch render it as the words the wise are made to say of Job, heading the closing indictment that Job be tried for answering after the manner of evil men.
Clarke reads it more roundly: no good arguing with a self-willed, self-conceited man; Job has spoken destitute of wisdom and discretion.

themes: the fault bounded to his speech

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers ‘O my Father, let Job be tried’ (addressed to God), notes Elihu’s words weighed no more with Job than the friends’, and mends the clause to ‘answering like wicked men.’
Wesley: try Job thoroughly, for his answers on behalf of wicked men; Clarke recoils — a harsh wish, the whole chapter destitute of mildness, and marvels a pious divine took Elihu for Jesus Christ.
Gill gives it as Elihu’s opinion left with the wise, noting Broughton’s ‘O my Father, let Job be tried.’

debates.question: Is Elihu’s demand a sober reproof or a cruel wish?

sides.position: the sober close of a well-meant reproof, or a prayer to God to try Job
a harsh, uncompassionate wish, out of keeping with a professed advocate of God

outliers.note: Judges the wish and the whole chapter nearly destitute of mildness and compassion, and finds it incredible that any could take Elihu, so speaking, for Jesus Christ.

themes: let Job be tried unto the end
my desire or O my Father
for wicked men or like wicked men

schools.summary: Wesley takes the charge as standing — Job grown obstinate, justifying himself and accusing God, his clapping insulting; Clarke turns wholly against Elihu, calling it a cruel, unfounded caustic, harsher than the friends, Elihu now in the tempest of words.
Gill softens it to a warning — ‘he may add’ — Job as yet guilty only of sins of ignorance, but if unchecked will proceed to presumptuous rebellion.

Henry sets the threefold indictment as Elihu means it — taking part with God’s enemies, insulting his friends, and speaking against God — closing with ‘I may fall into error, but I will not plunge into heresy.’
Ellicott glosses the gesture: Job clappeth his hands as though confident of victory in argument.

sides.position: a fair naming of Job’s obstinacy and rebellion against God
a warning against a rebellion not yet reached — Job as yet only mistaken
a cruel, unfounded caustic, harsher than the friends and unworthy of God’s advocate

outliers.note: Condemns the charge as ill-natured, cruel, and unfounded, more severe than the most inveterate of Job’s friends, and a sign that Elihu has fallen into the very tempest of words he began by disowning.

themes: the arbiter in the tempest of words
